did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens by blessing the Lord as “my rock” and describes him as the one who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war.

Did you know? David uses several images to describe the Lord’s protection: steadfast love, fortress, stronghold, refuge, and shield; he also describes the Lord as the one who subdues peoples under him.
Did you know? The question “What are human beings that you take notice of them?” emphasizes the contrast between human insignificance and the attention the Lord gives them.
Did you know? Human life is described in the psalm as a “breath” and as a passing shadow, images that emphasize its brevity and transience.
Did you know? The psalmist asks the Lord to part the heavens and come down, and even to touch the mountains so that they smoke—a powerful description of divine intervention in nature.
Did you know? The expression “from mighty waters” serves as a metaphor for great danger, from which the psalmist asks to be rescued from the hands of foreigners.
Did you know? The foreigners are described using two expressions associated with untrustworthiness: their mouths speak lies, and their right hands are “right hands of deceit.”
Did you know? David promises to sing a “new song” to the Lord and make music to him on a ten-stringed harp, meaning an instrument with ten strings.

Did you know? The Lord is described as the one who gives victory to kings and rescues David, his servant, from the deadly sword; verse 11 repeats the request to be rescued from the hands of foreigners.
Did you know? The psalm concludes by describing true happiness in a twofold statement: “Blessed are the people”—not only because of prosperity, family, and peace, but because the Lord is their God.
